summary: Proposes backwards-compatible extensions to Mobile IP to support reverse tunnels, so traffic from a mobile device goes back through its home network, which helps with routers that filter packets. It was replaced by RFC 3024.

eli5.summary: When you travel, your mail goes back to your home post office first, so it looks like it came from home.

questions: why reverse tunnel in mobile ip
what is reverse tunneling in mobile ip
how do mobile nodes send packets back
what is a care of address
subtitle: Tunneling data from mobile devices back through their home network

tldr.problem: Mobile IP uses tunneling from the home agent to the mobile node, but routers increasingly filter packets based on source address. A mobile node sending packets from abroad with its home address does not meet topological correctness requirements, causing packets to be dropped.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2344 adds a reverse tunnel from the mobile node's care-of address (where it is) back to its home agent. The RFC defines two delivery styles: Direct Delivery (the foreign agent intercepts unencapsulated packets) and Encapsulating Delivery Style (the mobile node encapsulates outgoing packets). Both methods ensure packets appear to come from topologically correct addresses.
tldr.outcome: Reverse tunneling allows mobile nodes to work with routers that filter by source address and supports multicast and broadcast delivery. RFC 2344 was replaced by RFC 3024, which consolidated and updated the specification.

facts.label: T bit
facts.value: Added to Mobility Agent Advertisement Extension and Registration Request

today: RFC 2344 was superseded by RFC 3024 in June 2000, which consolidated and updated the reverse tunneling specification. RFC 3024 is the current standard for reverse tunneling in Mobile IP.

sections.title: The Problem: Source Address Filtering
sections.content:
Mobile IP was designed so that a mobile node away from home can send and receive packets through a home agent, which is a server at the mobile node's home network. The home agent forwards incoming packets to the mobile node at its current location (the care-of address) via a forward tunnel.

However, the mobile node itself usually sends packets directly using its home address as the source. This violates a common security assumption: that packets are routed based on the destination address, not the source address. Modern routers use ingress filtering to reject packets whose source address does not match the network they came from. A packet sent from abroad with a home address as the source gets dropped.

The RFC proposes reverse tunneling to solve this. Instead of sending packets directly, the mobile node sends them back to the home agent through a tunnel from the care-of address. This way, the packet appears to come from the home network, satisfying source address filters.
sections.eli5: Guards at the border check that packages are coming from the right place. If your package leaves from another country with your home address, they throw it away. Reverse tunneling puts your package back in your home post office first, so guards let it through.

sections.title: How Reverse Tunneling Works
sections.content:
The RFC extends Mobile IP with a new bit, the T bit, in two places:

  • In the Mobility Agent Advertisement Extension, the T bit signals that a foreign agent supports reverse tunneling.
  • In the Registration Request, the T bit tells the home agent and foreign agent that the mobile node wants a reverse tunnel.

When a mobile node sees a foreign agent offering reverse tunneling, it sets the T bit and includes an optional Encapsulating Delivery Style Extension (type 130) to specify how it will send packets to the foreign agent.

The process is backwards-compatible: agents that do not understand the T bit ignore it. If an agent does support reverse tunneling but the mobile node does not request it, the agent MAY deny the registration with a new reply code.

Registration Requests with the T bit set MUST have the TTL field set to 255 in the IP header. This is a security measure: it prevents attackers more than one hop away from hijacking the reverse tunnel by posing as the mobile node.
sections.eli5: The mobile node tells its home and foreign agents: I want my outgoing mail to come back to the home office first. The agents check if they can do that. If they agree, they set up a secure tunnel.

sections.title: Two Delivery Styles
sections.content:
The RFC defines two ways to send packets from the mobile node to the foreign agent, each with trade-offs.

Direct Delivery Style: The mobile node designates the foreign agent as its default router and sends unencapsulated packets (with the home address as the source). The foreign agent detects these packets, encapsulates them, and tunnels them to the home agent. This is simple for the mobile node and uses minimal bandwidth on the link between them, but it only works for unicast (one-to-one) packets and does not allow selective routing.

Encapsulating Delivery Style: The mobile node itself encapsulates outgoing packets with an outer header destining them to the foreign agent. The foreign agent decapsulates, re-encapsulates with the foreign agent's address as the source, and tunnels to the home agent. This is more work for the mobile node but supports broadcast and multicast packets and allows selective reverse tunneling: the mobile node can send some packets directly (without encapsulation) to reach local resources without using the tunnel.

By default, both styles use IP in IP encapsulation (protocol number 4), but other methods negotiated at registration time MAY be used instead.
sections.eli5: Direct Delivery is like handing mail to the foreign agent and saying forward it. Encapsulating Delivery is like putting it in an envelope addressed to the foreign agent first, then the agent forwards it. The second way takes more work but lets you send packages to the local post office without the tunnel.

sections.title: Packet Headers and Formats
sections.content:
Both delivery styles follow the same encapsulation pattern for the reverse tunnel from the foreign agent to the home agent.

In Direct Delivery, the foreign agent receives packets with the mobile node's home address as the source and encapsulates them with a new outer header. The outer header has the foreign agent's care-of address as the source and the home agent's address as the destination. The protocol field is set to 4 (IP in IP). The inner packet is unchanged.

In Encapsulating Delivery, the mobile node sends a pre-encapsulated packet with its home address in the outer source, destined to the foreign agent. The foreign agent removes this encapsulation, then adds a new outer layer with the foreign agent's care-of address as the source and the home agent's address as the destination, again using IP in IP. The payload remains the mobile node's home address as the source.

In both cases, the home agent receives the reverse-tunneled packet, checks that the source of the outer header (the care-of address) matches a registered mobile binding with the inner source address (the home address), and then decapsulates and forwards the inner packet to the correspondent host. This binding check is a security measure to prevent injection of arbitrary packets into the network.
sections.eli5: The packet has two layers of wrapping. The inner label has the mobile node's home address. The outer label says it came from the foreign agent and is going to the home agent. When it arrives home, the home office unwraps it and forwards it to the real destination.

sections.title: Security and Robustness
sections.content:
Reverse tunneling inherits the security mechanisms of Mobile IP: authentication extensions must be present when there is a security association between two entities, and all registration protocol datagrams are authenticated.

The main risk is reverse tunnel hijacking: a malicious node could intercept the tunnel setup and redirect it elsewhere, or inject packets into the reverse tunnel to reach the home network. The RFC addresses this with several measures.

The requirement that mobile nodes set TTL to 255 in Registration Requests prevents attackers beyond one hop away from posing as a valid mobile node. The home agent MUST check that the outer source address (the care-of address) of a reverse-tunneled packet matches an active mobility binding with the given inner source (the home address). If no such binding exists, the packet is silently discarded and logged. This ensures that only packets from the mobile node's registered care-of address are accepted.

The RFC notes that network administrators might be concerned about filtering reverse-tunneled packets (IP in IP encapsulated traffic). However, the RFC cites the ingress filtering recommendation: reverse tunnels actually improve security tracking, because the outer source address now appears legitimate.
sections.eli5: There are guards to make sure only the real mobile node uses the tunnel. The TTL trick stops nearby attackers. The home agent checks that the package really came from the foreign agent with the right mobile node. If something looks wrong, the package is thrown away quietly.
